Intel Discloses $1.9B Classiq Deal Terms, With Up to $350M More at Stake
sum: Intel Corp. has agreed to acquire Classiq, an Israeli quantum-computing software developer, for roughly $1.9 billion plus as much as $350 million in contingent payments tied to performance milestones, according to the company's quarterly filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

The disclosure, made in Intel's third-quarter 10-Q, marks the first detailed look at the financial structure of a transaction announced on Oct. 26. The purchase price remains subject to customary adjustments, and the total potential consideration of about $2.25 billion sits close to the $2.3 billion valuation reported when the deal was unveiled.

Intel has not said which milestones would trigger the extra $350 million or how much of that amount it expects to pay. The filing also leaves open how the chipmaker will fund the purchase: it may settle in cash or in shares of common stock, and no decision on the mix has been disclosed. Intel said it has yet to complete its purchase accounting assessment, so no allocation among goodwill, identifiable intangibles and other items is available.
The agreement covers 100% of Classiq and is expected to close in the first half of 2027, pending regulatory approvals and other customary conditions.

Strategically, the deal would pair Classiq's software with Intel's quantum hardware program, which the company has funded since 2015 and which centers on silicon spin-qubit technology. Classiq's platform lets developers design and optimize quantum applications without managing the complexity of the underlying hardware, and it is built to run across multiple qubit technologies rather than a single processor type. Intel said the combination would support a full-stack quantum business, adding quantum processing units to a lineup that already spans CPUs, GPUs and application-specific chips.
Classiq raised $110 million in 2025 and later said IonQ, AMD and Qualcomm Ventures joined a subsequent funding round.

The disclosure landed during a difficult stretch for Intel shareholders. The stock closed at $90.47 on Oct. 26, the day the deal was announced, and had fallen to $52.25 by Nov. 5, a drop of about 42%. The steepest slide came on Oct. 30, when the shares lost nearly 29% following the company's quarterly results.

The company generated revenue of 16.5 billion US dollars, up 21 percent from a year earlier, while adjusted diluted earnings per share reached 0.52 US dollars, compared with 0.23 US dollars in the prior-year quarter. Intel said the quarter included its strongest data-center revenue growth in 15 years. Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said the company would continue disciplined investment in capacity and working capital while expecting the PC slowdown to continue at least through the first half of 2027.

Intel Foundry revenue increased 58 percent year over year to 6.7 billion US dollars. sum: Intel stock suffered historic declines due to weak PC demand and guidance missing expectations by up to $2 billion. Despite a surge earlier this year driven by government backing and Nvidia investment, supply bottlenecks in server CPUs forced Intel to divert 18A foundry capacity to mature nodes, risking its long-term manufacturing strategy. Technically oversold with an RSI of 22.95, the stock may see short-term bounces, but fundamental recovery requires stabilizing PC demand and securing external foundry orders. Key support levels stand at $55 and $50, while immediate resistance ranges from $60 to $66.

TradingKey - Intel (INTC) stock continued its severe adjustment. On the last trading day of October, the stock plunged 29%, marking its worst single-day performance since the 1970s; for the entire month, it fell by a cumulative 45%, making it the largest monthly decline on record for the company. Entering November, selling pressure showed no signs of abating, with the stock dropping another 8% on the first trading day, indicating that investor confidence in the company's short-term results and recovery prospects has yet to recover.

The immediate catalyst for this correction was Intel's guidance, which fell significantly short of Wall Street expectations. The company expects revenue for the current quarter to potentially miss market forecasts by $1 billion to $2 billion, with weak PC demand acting as the primary drag. Rising prices for memory and other components have not only driven up total computer costs but also dampened the willingness of consumers and enterprises to replace PCs. Since PC-related business still accounts for nearly half of Intel's revenue, the cooling in end-market demand can hardly be offset quickly by other business segments.

This stands in sharp contrast to market expectations a few months ago, after the U.S. government announced it would acquire about a 10% stake in Intel, followed by Nvidia (NVDA) investing another $5 billion, which further boosted market confidence that the company would gain capital support and improve its operations. Driven by this, Intel's stock price surged several-fold over a period of roughly 10 months, reaching a periodic high in June this year.

sum: Intel (INTC) has surged over 250% in 2026, reaching $140.05 amid optimism regarding foundry partnerships, notably with Apple and Microsoft. While 18A-P technology has entered risk production, significant revenue impact remains 12–18 months away. Despite BofA’s upgrade to a $160 target, Intel’s Q1 2026 net loss reflects an ongoing investment phase. Technicals remain neutral-bullish, with an upside breakout possible above $150.40. Key risks include execution delays in 18A yields, which could defer margin targets to 2028. Investors should monitor July 23 earnings for formal contract disclosures and concrete foundry volume commitments.

TradingKey - Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) is sitting at $140.05, holding the line on an ascending trend in the 4H timeframe following a run-up that has carried the stock from $36.90 at the beginning of 2026 to its highest level in 25 years, a gain of over 250% over the past half-year. The catalyst stack here is, to be frank, atypical for a turnaround story: President Trump publicly confirmed the Apple foundry deal on June 18; 18A-P entered risk production at the VLSI Symposium two days prior, right on schedule; Bank of America upgraded Intel from Underperform to Buy and hiked its price target to $160; and President Trump has repeatedly touted a 10% U.S. government stake alongside Nvidia and “TerraFab” (Elon Musk’s new company) onshoring. RSI is sitting at 62.55, neutral-bullish, with some room to run on the way up and no sign of bearish divergence yet. The charts look good. But whether investors are paying for a 2027-and-beyond revenue stream in a stock that is already up 250% is up for each of them to decide.

The Apple deal is real but it doesn’t mean shipping product yet. Intel and Apple have been in talks with an established timeline going back months before President Trump confirmed the foundry deal on June 18: Bloomberg reported on May 5 that talks had begun, and shares rallied 14% that day; the Wall Street Journal reported on an initial agreement in early May, and shares hit their previous all-time high on May 11.

sum: Options traders are bracing for a double-digit move in Intel Corp (NASDAQ:INTC) shares when the chipmaker reports third-quarter 2026 results after the closing bell on Thursday, a bet that lands just below the largest implied swing on a busy week of corporate earnings.

The market is pricing an implied move of 10.54% for Intel, according to options-derived estimates compiled in a preview of the week's biggest reports. That places the semiconductor company second on a list of ten major names ranked by expected volatility, behind only memory maker Sandisk Corp (NASDAQ:SNDK) at 11.71%.

Intel's setup is unusual because it pairs a steep implied move with a stock that has already run hard. Shares closed Friday at $86.96, up 117.1% year to date, yet they remain roughly 39% below the 52-week high of $142.35, a gap that suggests investors are still debating how much of the turnaround is already reflected in the price.

The run-up has a clear catalyst. Intel joined Elon Musk's Terafab chip project on April 7, the first major outside commitment for a foundry business that had previously made chips only for itself, and the stock more than doubled that month, its best on record. Musk later confirmed that Terafab would use Intel's 14A process. In early October, Musk said Terafab was in "just discussions" with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) and that "something may come of it"; Wall Street analysts said a TSMC role would add competition for Intel's foundry ambitions, and the shares fell 3% on Oct. 5 and another 3% the next day, according to CNBC.

Consensus estimates call for earnings of 39 cents a share on revenue of $16.45 billion, compared with 23 cents and $13.65 billion in the same quarter a year earlier. That implies earnings per share growth of about 70.3% and revenue growth of roughly 20.5%, based on estimates cited by LSEG data.

The consensus sits close to Intel's own forecast. In July, the company guided third-quarter revenue to $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion and non-GAAP earnings of 38 cents a share, with a 42% non-GAAP gross margin at the midpoint of the revenue range. The revenue estimate is above the midpoint of that range, and the EPS estimate is a penny above guidance.

$Intel (INTC.US)$ shares headed for a fourth straight session of declines Tuesday and the latest downward move had little to do with short sellers, but was driven by renewed concerns about the capital needed for the AI buildout.

The selling began after CEO Lip-Bu Tan told a conference in Singapore Monday that access to capital — not chips, memory or power — is now the biggest constraint on the AI buildout. $Broadcom (AVGO.US)$ 's Hock Tan, sharing the stage, went further and likened some AI investors to casino gamblers who "have no clue what they are investing in," in comments reported by Bloomberg.

When the heads of two of the industry's biggest suppliers start questioning who is paying for the boom, holders listen — and Intel, Broadcom, $NVIDIA (NVDA.US)$, $Micron Technology (MU.US)$, $SanDisk (SNDK.US)$, $Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.US)$ and the $PHLX Semiconductor Index (.SOX.US)$ all ended Mondaydown.

Exchange data tracked by moomoo shows 7.07 million borrowed Intel shares were sold short on Monday — 9.54% of the 74.17 million shares traded, well below the 13.09% average. Short selling means borrowing shares to sell them now in the hope of buying them back cheaper later; a low short share on a down day means the bears weren't the ones doing the damage. The absolute number tells the same story: Monday's short volume sits near the lowest in more than a month while September's heaviest shorting days — back when the stock traded above $120 — were roughly three times heavier. The bears positioned at the top and have stopped adding, because they haven't needed to.

Instead they are sitting on their winnings. Short interest — the total pile of outstanding short bets that haven’t been closed— has climbed to about 3.2% of the float, the highest in more than a year. Nobody is covering into the decline, which would have cushioned the fall, and nobody is pressing new bets either. The professionals are simply watching the longs do the work for them.
And the longs are doing plenty of work. A net $68.22 million flowed out of the stock on Monday, with selling beating buying in every order size from institutional blocks down to retail-sized trades.

What Is The Case For Waiting On Intel Stock?
sum: Intel (INTC) stock is up about 334% over the past year, against 17.1% for the S&P 500. Buying at $127.39 a share means believing two things: operating profit keeps climbing, and sales beat Intel’s own forecasts again. Is it already too late to own Intel after a run like that?

Intel’s operating profit is recovering, but it is starting from a loss. Operating margin, the share of sales left after running the business, was 7.6% over the last twelve months. A year earlier, the business ran at an operating loss equal to 8.3% of sales.

Even with that operating profit, Intel still posted a net loss of $11.3 billion over the last twelve months. With earnings negative, the usual price-to-earnings ratio means nothing here. Cash flow is the other yardstick. The stock costs 30.4 times the operating cash flow, the cash the business brings in, against 14.6 for the S&P 500.

The stock also trades at 8.0 times sales. Over ten years, that multiple has ranged from 1.5 to 12.5. Intel’s operating margin reached 34% at its best in that decade. So today’s multiple rests on sales that earn far less than they once did.

One drag is Intel Foundry, the factory arm. It posted an operating loss of $2.1 billion in the second quarter of 2026. Management said on the July 23, 2026 call, that new chips such as Panther Lake still earn below the company’s average margin. Those chips are early in their life cycle, management said. With operating margin still far below its best, today’s price depends mostly on sales.
Intel’s sales beat its own forecast in the second quarter of 2026. Revenue for that quarter was $16.1 billion, $1.8 billion above the midpoint of the guide.

For the third quarter, management guided revenue of $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion. The analyst consensus for that quarter is about $16.7 billion, inside that range but near its top. So the price appears to assume a quarter near the top of the guide.

sum: Nvidia's $5 billion Intel investment has produced an extraordinary paper gain, but the timeline matters. The companies announced the investment and product collaboration on September 18, 2025. Intel's SEC filing shows that NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) actually completed the purchase on December 26, 2025, acquiring 214,776,632 Intel shares at $23.28 each for $5 billion. Nvidia's June 30, 2026 13F valued the same share count at $29.989 billion. That is a large unrealized gain; it does not establish that the commercial partnership has already succeeded. Subtracting the original cost leaves an unrealized gain of about $24.989 billion at quarter-end, an amount that will move with Intel's share price.
Intel Corp.'s headquarters, the Robert Noyce Building in Santa Clara, California. Photo from Intel Corp website

The companies said Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) would build Nvidia-custom x86 CPUs for Nvidia AI infrastructure and x86 system-on-chips integrating Nvidia RTX GPU chiplets for PCs. The latest official disclosures reviewed still describe those custom products as a collaboration under development, so the investment's market value is ahead of the operating evidence.

The bull case is an ecosystem bridge. Nvidia can pair its accelerators, networking, and NVLink with an enormous x86 software base. Intel gains a powerful partner and a route to more valuable data-center and client packages. If the jointly developed products arrive on schedule and win meaningful volume, both companies could strengthen their positions across heterogeneous computing.

The countercase is execution. Intel Foundry posted a $2.089 billion operating loss in the second quarter. Intel also reported an $11.033 billion GAAP net loss attributable to the company, largely distorted by a $12.529 billion mark-to-market loss on shares held in escrow for the U.S. government; non-GAAP net income was $2.197 billion. The accounting charge should not be mistaken for foundry performance, but the segment loss shows that manufacturing economics remain difficult. Product delays or weak adoption could keep the alliance strategically interesting without making it profitable. At the same time, Intel's revenue rose 25% year over year to $16.128 billion, so the quarter was not simply an operating collapse.

And hot might be an understatement. Intel shares had nearly tripled in 2026 before the offering, giving management a golden window to raise billions without taking on another mountain of debt. Cheap for existing shareholders? Not exactly. The expanded deal could equal roughly 3.5% of Intel's market value, making dilution impossible to shrug off. Intel now has more ammunition, but the market has already priced in a lot of success. The next leg higher will need something much harder than another capital raise: major foundry wins, tighter spending and proof that Intel can turn its manufacturing billions into real returns.

Investing.com — Intel Corporation shares advanced 3.6% in pre-open trading as investors responded to a combination of manufacturing progress and upbeat analyst commentary that supported the company’s foundry-focused turnaround plan.

The key catalyst was a reported step-change in yields on Intel’s 18A leading-edge manufacturing node. Yields climbed to roughly 85% from approximately 65% in the prior quarter, putting the process just behind TSMC’s N2 node at around 90%, while significantly outperforming Samsung’s rival technology. This improvement is being viewed as a critical proof point for Intel’s process roadmap.

In a separate development, reports indicated that production of Intel’s upcoming Nova Lake chips is being transitioned in-house. Bringing this next-generation product under Intel’s own manufacturing umbrella is being interpreted as a sign of rising internal conviction in the 18A process and a move that reduces exposure to external foundry providers.

On Wall Street, KeyBanc added to the positive momentum by lifting its price target on Intel shares to $155 from $110 while reiterating an Overweight rating. The firm’s analyst emphasized that the improved 18A yields are reshaping the overall investment narrative around the stock.

sum: The slump came after Intel shares jumped 216% in the three months ended June 30, its biggest quarterly gain ever. The gamma exposure snapshot showed a notable put wall clustered near $130, where large open interest in put options had previously provided some support.

When the stock breached that level, market makers who sell puts to option buyers typically hedge by selling shares or futures, creating a feedback loop that magnifies downside moves. This gamma dynamic, which describes how quickly an option’s delta changes with the underlying stock price, turned from stabilizing to destabilizing once the wall broke.

This options-driven selling unfolded against a backdrop of profit-taking across the chip sector. The $PHLX Semiconductor Index (.SOX.US)$ fell 5%, with $Teradyne (TER.US)$, $KLA Corp (KLAC.US)$, $Lam Research (LRCX.US)$ and $Micron Technology (MU.US)$ leading the declines. Intel has delivered one of the market’s strongest turnarounds, with the stock more than doubling year-to-date on AI infrastructure demand, foundry progress, and partnerships including a deal tied to Apple chips.

Recent analyst actions, such as Cantor Fitzgerald raising its price target, helped fuel the the bullish narrative seen in the first half of the year around the U.S.-based manufacturing and CPU strength in AI inference. Yet after such a rapid run, end-of-quarter rebalancing and rotation out of overheated names weighed on sentiment.

At the same time, the volatility smile across near-term expirations highlighted elevated demand for downside protection, pushing implied volatility even higher and making further swings more expensive to hedge

Implied volatility reached 98%, reflecting extreme uncertainty among traders. This move came amid a broader cooling in semiconductor sentiment after an extraordinary rally earlier in the year that sent the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index climbing 88% in the second quarter, also a record for the benchmark.

Intel’s volatility term structure revealed short-dated implied volatility starting above 100% before declining toward longer expirations, a pattern typical when traders anticipate near-term events but expect calmer conditions later.

sum: Intel (INTC) is once again back in the Wall Street headlines. This happened when Nancy Pelosi's latest filing showed 200 Intel call options with a $50 strike price and a March 19, 2027, expiration date, valued between $1.5 million and $6 million. That is the kind of move that makes traders lean in. But Intel is still a real business story, not a political trading story.

The company makes server chips, client chips, and foundry services, and the stock still lives or dies on execution. The key question is simple. Has Intel improved enough to deserve fresh money, or has the rally already done the work for you?

That kind of move did not come from one filing. It came from a long list of catalysts. AI demand helped. So did the U.S. government stake, SoftBank's (SFTBY) backing, Nvidia's (NVDA) support, and the market's growing belief that Intel can still matter in CPUs and manufacturing. More recently, the Apple (AAPL) chatter and BofA's "Buy" upgrade with a $135 target kept the momentum alive.

This is where the story gets tricky. INTC stock trades at about 6 times forward sales, which looks cheaper than Lam Research (LRCX) at 11.8 times and Applied Materials (AMAT) at 9.1 times. But on earnings, Intel is still rich. One recent comparison put Intel's forward P/E at over 95, far above healthy chip peers. That tells you the stock is not a clean bargain. It is a turnaround bet. Investors are paying for a future that has not fully shown up in profits yet.
